title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
hookLine: a king with everything and one longing, and why Hindus bring their longings to the sacred fire
carry: yajna: bringing what you lack to the sacred fire
tomorrow: who was the forest boy the rain followed?

lines: A CITY WORKING AS IT SHOULD.
cards: The first thing Valmiki gives us is a city. Ayodhya, on the river Sarayu, in the land of Kosala.
Wide straight roads sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers, gates and arches, music, merchants, horses, elephants, full granaries.
In his telling, nobody there is greedy, nobody lies, nobody is without learning or without food. A city working as it should.
And at its center sits a king who has everything, and who can't sleep for wanting the one thing he doesn't have.

teach.b: The king is Dasharatha, of the line of Ikshvaku. His name means ten chariots. He's wise, generous, a well-known warrior, guided by great counselors like the sage Vasishtha.
He has three chief queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And he has no son. For a king in the epic's world, that isn't only personal sorrow.
It's the line, the ancestors' rites, the kingdom's future. So Dasharatha decides: I will perform the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, for the sake of sons. Notice how he does it.

He lays out his grief to his priests and ministers, and asks. They approve. And his charioteer, Sumantra, remembers an old prophecy about a young sage named Rishyashringa, whose story is strange enough for tomorrow.
Now the teaching under the scene.
A sacrifice, a yajna, is the oldest form of Hindu worship: offerings poured into a fire with sacred words. Agni, the fire, is the messenger who carries them to the gods.
The Bhagavad Gita puts it simply: nourish the gods with sacrifice, and they will nourish you. Give, and receive; a circle. Hindu families still live inside that circle.
At a wedding, the couple walks around the fire. Before moving into a new home, many families hold a havan: a small fire, ghee and grain poured in, with svaha at each offering.
So the Ramayana's first real scene isn't heroic at all. It's a good man admitting what he lacks, asking the people around him, and bringing his longing to the sacred fire.

how: Ayodhya, on the Sarayu river in today's Uttar Pradesh, is revered in Hindu tradition as Rama's birthplace; and the yajna lives on in Hindu homes as the havan, a small fire offering held for weddings, housewarmings and other big days.

o: a fire rite to end a long drought in Ayodhya
a king's offering of thanks after a great victory
the horse rite the childless king holds for sons

s: Dasharatha decides on the sacrifice without consulting anyone
he lays out his grief and plan to his priests and ministers first.
in a yajna, offerings are poured into a sacred fire
Agni, the fire, carries them to the gods. families still do it at a havan.
Sumantra links the moment to an old prophecy
a young sage named Rishyashringa will bring sons to the king.

games.q: you're Dasharatha. you have everything a king could want, except a son. what do you do?
o: decide on a great sacrifice, with your counselors' blessing.
go to war to win glory instead.
games.why: he resolves on the ashvamedha, a great yajna, for the sake of sons, and asks his priests and ministers first. they approve.

practice: At a havan, each offering goes into the fire with one word: svaha. Let one longing come up, something you've wanted a long time, and hold it honestly.
If you pray, offer it on an out-breath, silently saying svaha, and let the fire have it. If you don't, simply name it, then name one person you could ask for help, as Dasharatha did.

wordCard.voice: Dasharatha's sacrifice. The great horse sacrifice the childless king of Ayodhya decides on, with his counselors, for the sake of sons.

orig.note: Sanskrit aśvamedha: the horse sacrifice, a great royal Vedic rite.

carryVoice: Your line: yajna, bringing what you lack to the sacred fire. Even a king with everything had something to offer up. That's day four hundred ninety-five.
